passages.text: Exploring functional and structural features of chemically related natural prenylated hydroquinone and benzoic acid from <italic>Piper crassinervium</italic> (Piperaceae) on bacterial peroxiredoxin inhibition

Multiple drug resistance (MDR) bacterial strains are responsible by 1.2 million of human deaths all over the world. <sentence_start/>The pathogens possess efficient enzymes which are able to mitigate the toxicity of reactive oxygen species (ROS) produced by some antibiotics and the host immune cells. <sentence_start/>Among them, the bacterial peroxiredoxin alkyl hydroperoxide reductase C (AhpC) is able to decompose efficiently several kinds of hydroperoxides. <sentence_start/>To decompose their substrates AhpC use a reactive cysteine residue (peroxidatic cysteine-Cys<sub>P</sub>) that together with two other polar residues (Thr/Ser and Arg) comprise the catalytic triad of these enzymes and are involved in the substrate targeting/stabilization to allow a bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (S<sub>N</sub>2) reaction. <sentence_start/>Additionally to the high efficiency the AhpC is very abundant in the cells and present virulent properties in some bacterial species. <sentence_start/>Despite the importance of AhpC in bacteria, few studies aimed at using natural compounds as inhibitors of this class of enzymes. <sentence_start/>Some natural products were identified as human isoforms, presenting as common characteristics a bulk hydrophobic moiety and an α, β-unsaturated carbonylic system able to perform a thiol-Michael reaction. <sentence_start/>In this work, we evaluated two chemically related natural products: 1,4-dihydroxy-2-(3’,7’-dimethyl-1’-oxo-2’<italic>E</italic>,6’-octadienyl) benzene (<bold>C1</bold>) and 4-hydroxy-2-(3’,7’-dimethyl-1’-oxo-2’<italic>E</italic>,6’-octadienyl) benzoic acid (<bold>C2</bold>), both were isolated from branches <italic>Piper crassinervium</italic> (Piperaceae), over the peroxidase activity of AhpC from <italic>Pseudomonas aeruginosa</italic> (PaAhpC) and <italic>Staphylococcus epidermidis</italic> (SeAhpC). <sentence_start/>By biochemical assays we show that although both compounds can perform the Michael addition reaction, only compound <bold>C2</bold> was able to inhibit the PaAhpC peroxidase activity but not SeAhpC, presenting IC<sub>50</sub> = 20.3 μM. <sentence_start/>SDS-PAGE analysis revealed that the compound was not able to perform a thiol-Michael addition, suggesting another inhibition behavior. <sentence_start/>Using computer-assisted simulations, we also show that an acidic group present in the structure of compound <bold>C2</bold> may be involved in the stabilization by polar interactions with the Thr and Arg residues from the catalytic triad and several apolar interactions with hydrophobic residues. <sentence_start/>Finally, <bold>C2</bold> was not able to interfere in the peroxidase activity of the isoform Prx2 from humans or even the thiol proteins of the Trx reducing system from <italic>Escherichia coli</italic> (EcTrx and EcTrxR), indicating specificity for <italic>P</italic>. <italic>aeruginosa</italic> AhpC.
Introduction

Bacteria resistance to antibacterial drugs may be directly related to oxidative stress since antibiotics from different classes have the common ability to generate reactive oxygen species (ROS), damaging macromolecules, especially DNA [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref001" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1401876111" pmid="24803433" pmcid="PMC4034191" count="1">1</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref002" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cbi.2020.109023" pmid="32097615" count="1">2</citation>]. <sentence_start/>ROS are also produced by host immune cells to fight pathogen infections, and studies suggest that inhibition of antioxidant enzymes is deleterious to pathogens infection and establishment [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref003" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.redox.2021.102075" pmid="34315109" pmcid="PMC8327333" count="1">3</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Bacteria cells possess several antioxidant enzymes able to decompose ROS, including the typical 2-Cys peroxiredoxins, so called AhpCs [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref004" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00253-021-11360-5" pmid="34258640" count="1">4</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These enzymes are very abundant in bacteria and are considered virulence factors to some species, indicating they play an important role in pathogenesis [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref003" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.redox.2021.102075" pmid="34315109" pmcid="PMC8327333" count="1">3</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref005" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12275-009-0130-x" pmid="19851736" count="1">5</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref010" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1099/00221287-144-10-2687" pmid="9802010" count="1">10</citation>]. <sentence_start/>AhpC is the abbreviation used for alkyl hydroperoxide reductase subunit C, referring to its discovery, since the bacterial strains carrying deletions of <italic>ahpC</italic> gene were very sensitive to organic hydroperoxides [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref011" ref-type="bibr" pmid="2643600" count="1">11</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Later studies revealed that AhpC are also very reactive to several kinds of hydroperoxide, such as hydrogen peroxide (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) and peroxynitrite (NOO<sup>-</sup>) [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref012" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.0708308105" pmid="18165315" pmcid="PMC2448816" count="1">12</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref014" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fmicb.2019.01483" pmid="31338075" pmcid="PMC6626918" count="1">14</citation>].

The peroxidatic mechanism of typical 2-Cys Prx is based on a conserved catalytic triad (TC) composed of a reactive cysteine residue (peroxidatic cysteine-Cys<sub>P</sub>), an Arg, and a Thr or Ser. <sentence_start/>The mechanistic importance of the catalytic triad residues has been well studied experimentally, and it is based on an intricate hydrogen bonds network involved in the hydroperoxide decomposition [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref015" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jmb.2010.07.022" pmid="20643143" pmcid="PMC2941395" count="1">15</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref016" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/tx100413v" pmid="21391663" count="1">16</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The Arg and Thr/Ser are able to stabilize the Cys<sub>P</sub> in the thiolate state (Cys<sub>P</sub>-S<sup>-</sup>) by hydrogen bonds, decreasing its p<italic>K</italic><sub>a</sub>. <sentence_start/>These residues are also involved in the orientation and activation of the hydroperoxide molecule (R-OOH) by hydrogen bonds network, allowing the optimal reactivity of Cys<sub>P</sub> through a S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref015" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jmb.2010.07.022" pmid="20643143" pmcid="PMC2941395" count="1">15</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref016" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/tx100413v" pmid="21391663" count="1">16</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Together, this molecular mechanism culminates in Cys<sub>P</sub> oxidation to cysteine sulfenic acid (CysP-SOH) and the release of the leaving group (R-OH) (<bold>Fig 1</bold>). <sentence_start/>Computer-assisted simulations of the reaction of different Prxs with H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gave further insights into the mechanism of catalysis at a molecular level, supporting the catalytic mechanism proposed [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref017" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M111.232355" pmid="21385867" pmcid="PMC3093878" count="1">17</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref018" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/c4cc02899f" pmid="25045760" pmcid="PMC4336542" count="1">18</citation>].
Fig 1
Molecular interactions and peroxide decomposition reactions of 2-Cys Prx.

The thiolate nucleophilicity of peroxidatic cysteine (Cys<sub>P</sub>) is increased by hydrogen bonds with the catalytic triad Arg and Thr residues <bold>(i)</bold>. <sentence_start/>The hydroperoxide (Hpx) is trapped by the Arg hydrogen bond which is able to target the Hpx to the Prx active site <bold>(ii)</bold>. <sentence_start/>The shift of the Arg and Thr hydrogen bonds from the Cys<sub>P</sub> thiolate to the substrate stabilizes the Hpx and increase the thiolate reactivity enabling the S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism <bold>(iii)</bold>. <sentence_start/>After the catalytic reaction, the Cys<sub>P</sub> is oxidized to cysteine sulfenic acid (Cys<sub>P</sub>-SOH) and the release of the leaving group (R-OH, meaning a water molecule in the case of hydrogen peroxide, or the alcohol derivative, in the case of organic hydroperoxides) is assisted by polar interaction with Arg <bold>(iv</bold>). <sentence_start/>The cysteine sulfenic acid formation triggers structural changes which allow the condensation among Cys<sub>P</sub>-SOH with Cys<sub>R</sub>-SH <bold>(v)</bold> resulting in the disulfide formation and concomitant release of a water molecule <bold>(vi)</bold>. <sentence_start/>The asterisk (*) in Cys<sub>R</sub>, denotes the adjacent subunit of the homodimer.

The typical 2-Cys Prx are obligate homodimers. <sentence_start/>After hydroperoxide decomposition, the Cys<sub>P</sub> forms an intramolecular disulfide with a second cysteine residue (resolving Cys; Cys<sub>R</sub>) found in the adjacent subunit. <sentence_start/>Despite that, the minimum catalytic unit of 2-Cys Prx has been homodimer, when these enzymes are in the reduced state (Cys<sub>P</sub>-S<sup>-</sup>) they are found as α 2 [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref005" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12275-009-0130-x" pmid="19851736" count="1">5</citation>] decamers, forming a structure that resembles a doughnut [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref020" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/bi012173m" pmid="11969410" count="1">20</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In enzymes containing Thr as part of the catalytic triad, the peroxide decomposition with consequent oxidation of the cysteines to disulfide triggers conformational changes that result in the decamer disruption in dimers [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref019" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1089/ars.2010.3624" pmid="20969484" pmcid="PMC3125576" count="1">19</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref021" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.1080405" pmid="12714747" count="1">21</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Conversely to 2-Cys Prx containing Ser in the CT, the disulfide formation occurs without significant quaternary structure transition [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref022" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/antiox10071032" pmid="34202406" pmcid="PMC8300647" count="1">22</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref023" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/srep33133" pmid="27629822" pmcid="PMC5024103" count="1">23</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The reducing agent of typical 2-Cys Prx are represented by the thioredoxin system or by the AhpF which are able to reduce the Prx disulfide, restoring the reactive state [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref023" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/srep33133" pmid="27629822" pmcid="PMC5024103" count="1">23</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref024" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/antiox10071032" pmid="34202406" pmcid="PMC8300647" count="1">24</citation>].

Despite the apparent AhpC importance to the establishment and survival of pathogenic bacteria in hosts, few studies aimed at finding inhibitors to these enzymes [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref025" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/ja909150y" pmid="20433172" count="1">25</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref026" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acs.chemrestox.2c00049" pmid="35537067" count="1">26</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Some isoforms of typical Prx 2-Cys are overexpressed in some human genetic diseases, including cancer and biological processes as inflammation, and some inhibitory macro and micro-molecules, such as antibodies and natural or synthetic low molecular weight compounds, have already been characterized as eukaryotic counterparts [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref027" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nm.2749" pmid="22610280" count="1">27</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref034" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4049/jimmunol.1700796" pmid="30185517" count="1">34</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A common feature shared among low molecular weight compounds is a very bulky carbon skeleton, which may resemble natural oxidant substrates as organic hydroperoxides. <sentence_start/>Among the natural compounds identified to eukaryotic isoforms, three of them are <italic>ent</italic>-kauranes diterpenes (adenanthin, JM-202, and parvifoline AA). <sentence_start/>The inhibitory action of these compounds is based on the alkylation of the catalytic cysteines through a thiol-Michael addition involving an α,β-unsaturated carbonylic system from the inhibitors [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref029" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nchembio.935" pmid="22484541" count="1">29</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref030" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1089/ars.2016.6703" pmid="27650197" pmcid="PMC5510680" count="1">30</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref033" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.chembiol.2019.04.003" pmid="31130519" count="1">33</citation>].

As part of our continuous studies concerning the identification of natural inhibitors of peroxiredoxins, we here isolated two chemically related natural compounds- 1,4-dihydroxy-2-(3’,7’-dimethyl-1’-oxo-2’<italic>E</italic>,6’-octadienyl) benzene (<bold>C1</bold>) and 4-hydroxy-2-(3’,7’-dimethyl-1’-oxo-2’<italic>E</italic>,6’-octadienyl) benzoic acid (<bold>C2</bold>) from branches of <italic>Piper crassinervium</italic> (Piperaceae). <sentence_start/>These chemicals were tested over the AhpCs containing Thr or Ser as part of the catalytic triad, using recombinant enzymes from <italic>Pseudomonas aeruginosa</italic> and <italic>Staphylococcus epidermidis</italic>, opportunistics Gram -negative and -positive bacteria involved in hospital acquired infections. <sentence_start/>Using biochemical approaches, we identified compound <bold>C2</bold> as a novel natural product with inhibitory properties over PaAhpC but not over SeAhpC, that presents IC<sub>50</sub> in the order of 20.3 μM. <sentence_start/>We also demonstrated that the inhibitory properties were not due to the thiol-Michael addition mechanism over the catalytic cysteines, since the intramolecular disulfide formation of the enzyme was preserved. <sentence_start/>We also evaluated the inhibitory effect of the compound <bold>C2</bold> over the human isoform Prx2 and the thiol proteins Trx and TrxR from bacteria, and no significant inhibition was detected in the tested conditions, suggesting specificity to PaAhpC. Finally, we executed computer assisted molecular simulations to investigate a possible mode of binding, which revealed that compound <bold>C2</bold> is maintained in the active site by several non-polar interactions with residues of the PaAhpC active site microenvironment comprising three subunits of the decamer. <sentence_start/>Curiously <bold>C2</bold> possess physicochemical characteristics that resemble organic peroxides found in biological systems that are derived from aromatic compounds or long chain molecules, such as nitrogenous bases and lipids hydroperoxides and, ultimately, may mimics these kinds of biological substrates. <sentence_start/>Altogether, our results reveal a novel class of inhibitory natural compounds able to exert activity over the bacterial PaAhpC.
Experimental
General

Chromatographic separation procedures were performed using silica gel (Merck, 230-400 mesh) and silica gel 60 PF<sub>254</sub> (Merck) for column separation and for analytical (0.50mm) TLC, respectively. <sentence_start/>NMR spectra were recorded on a Varian Inova 500 spectrometer, operating at 500 MHz (<sup>1</sup>H nuclei) and 125 MHz (<sup>13</sup>C nuclei). <sentence_start/>CDCl<sub>3</sub> (Aldrich) was used as a solvent whereas tetramethylsilane (TMS) was employed as an internal standard. <sentence_start/>ESI-HRMS were recorded on a Bruker Daltonics MicroTOF QII spectrometer acquired with ESI (electrospray ionization) in both positive and negative ion mode. <sentence_start/>All solvents and reagents were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA) and Thermo Scientific (Logan, UT, USA).
Plant material

Branches of <italic>P</italic>. <italic>crassinervium</italic> were collected at Parque Estadual Fontes do Ipiranga, São Paulo State, Brazil and identified by Dr. Guilherme M. Antar from the Instituto de Biociências of Universidade de São Paulo (IB-USP), receiving the registration code SISGEN A4123E4. <sentence_start/>A voucher specimen (SPF 218827) was deposited in the Herbarium of IB-USP, São Paulo, SP, Brazil.
Extraction and isolation of the constituents

Dried and powdered branches (85 g) were exhaustively extracted with <italic>n</italic>-hexane at room temperature. <sentence_start/>The solvent of combined <italic>n</italic>-hexane was evaporated under reduced pressure to afford 747 mg of crude extract. <sentence_start/>Part of this material (670 mg) was chromatographed over a silica-gel column, eluted with increasing amounts of EtOAc in <italic>n</italic>-hexane, to afford pure <bold>C1</bold> (79.5 mg) and <bold>C2</bold> (44.2 mg).
Recombinant proteins

<italic>P</italic>. <italic>aeruginosa</italic> AhpC (PaAhpC), <italic>S</italic>. <italic>epidermidis</italic> AhpC (SeAhpC), and the Trx system from <italic>Escherichia coli</italic> (EcTrx and EcTrxR) were previously obtained [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref022" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/antiox10071032" pmid="34202406" pmcid="PMC8300647" count="1">22</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The expression of the human Prx2 (HsPrx2) and <italic>Saccharomyces cerevisiae</italic> Trx system (ScTrx1 and ScTrxR1) were performed as previously described by Truzzi and colleagues [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref035" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.RA119.008825" pmid="31366734" pmcid="PMC6755790" count="1">35</citation>].
Protein expression and purification

Transformed <italic>E</italic>. <italic>coli</italic> BL21 (DE3) cells containing pET15b-<italic>pa_ahpc</italic>, pET15b-<italic>se_ahpc</italic>, pET15b-<italic>ec_trx</italic>, pET15b-<italic>ec_trxr</italic>, pET28b-<italic>hs_</italic>prx2, pET15b-<italic>sc_trx1</italic> and pPROEX-<italic>sctrxr1</italic> were grown overnight at 37°C in 100 mL of medium LB (10% tryptone, 5% NaCl and 5% yeast extract) containing 100 μg/mL of ampicillin and then transferred to 1 L of fresh LB containing ampicillin (100 μg/mL) and grown to OD<sub>600</sub> = 0.6-0.8. <sentence_start/>Recombinant protein expression was induced by IPTG addition to a final concentration of 1 mM for 3 hours at 37°C. <sentence_start/>The cells were harvested by centrifugation at 4.000 × <italic>g</italic>/4°C/20 min, and the pellet was suspended with start buffer (20 mM sodium phosphate pH 7.4; 300 mM NaCl; 20 mM imidazole) containing PMSF (1 mM). <sentence_start/>Cell disruptions were performed by sonication (30% amplitude/ 24 cycles of 5 seconds and resting for 15 seconds in an ice bath, and nucleic acids were removed using streptomycin sulfate ([Final] = 1%). <sentence_start/>The suspensions were clarified by filtration (45μm membrane; Merck-Millipore) and following centrifugation (45 min/4°C/12.000 g) and the protein extracts free of nucleic acids were collected.
Determination of enzyme concentrations

Protein concentrations were measured by spectrophotometry at λ = 280 nm by the molar extinction coefficient using the ProtParam tool ( ). <sentence_start/>The enzyme abbreviations, Uniprot codes and enzyme properties are presented in Table 1.
Treatment of the enzymes with compounds C1 and C2

Enzyme samples [100 μM] were reduced with 5mM dithiothreitol (DTT) for 30 minutes at 25°C and desalted using PD10 columns (Cytiva Life Sciences, Marlborough, MA, USA), quantified, and the protein concentration were adjusted to 10 μM and treated with 50 M equivalents of compounds <bold>C1</bold> or <bold>C2</bold> for one hour at room temperature. <sentence_start/>As control of cysteine alkylation/enzyme inactivation, the Prx were treated with N-ethylmaleimide (NEM) 1h/RT. <sentence_start/>Finally, the treated proteins were desalted again to remove excess of the compounds and quantified again for use in subsequent assays.
NADPH coupled oxidation assay to test inhibitory properties of compounds C1 and C2

The inhibitory properties of compounds <bold>C1</bold> and <bold>C2</bold> on PaAhpC and SeAhpC peroxidase activity were tested using the <italic>E</italic>. <italic>coli</italic> Trx system by the coupled NADPH oxidation assay as previously described [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref022" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/antiox10071032" pmid="34202406" pmcid="PMC8300647" count="1">22</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Briefly: 3 μM of PaAhpC or SeAhpC was added to a mix containing 6 μM of EcTrx, 0.9 μM of EcTrxR, 150 μM of NADPH, in 50 mM HEPES pH 7.4 buffer, 1 mM DTPA and 100 μM sodium azide, and then incubated for 5 minutes at 37°C. <sentence_start/>The reactions were initiated by the addition of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (500 μM) and NADPH decay were monitored spectrophotometrically at 340 nm. <sentence_start/>As negative controls are represented by reactions without AhpC are (negative control), or AhpC pretreated with NEM (40 μM) (inhibition control), proteins without pretreatment (positive control), and proteins pretreated either with compounds <bold>C1</bold> and <bold>C2</bold>. <sentence_start/>To evaluate the inhibitory activity of compound <bold>C2</bold> over the human peroxiredoxin isoform were used human HsPrx2 (5 μM) and the heterologous yeast Trx system (ScTrx1, 10 μM and ScTrxR1, 0.2 μM).
Analysis of protein sequences and crystallographic structures

Protein alignments were performed using Clustal Ω [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref036" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/msb.2011.75" pmid="21988835" pmcid="PMC3261699" count="1">36</citation>], and the graphical representations were generated using JalView [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref037" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btp033" pmid="19151095" pmcid="PMC2672624" count="1">37</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Molecular crystallographic structures representations were made using the PyMol ( /).
Molecular docking approaches

Molecular dockings were performed using the coordinates 4MA9 from <italic>S</italic>. <italic>typhimurium</italic> AhpC obtained from the Protein Data Bank. <sentence_start/>Three-dimensional structures of compounds <bold>C1</bold> and <bold>C2</bold> were constructed using MolView [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref038" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/0263-7855(94)00019-o" pmid="7619787" count="1">38</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Docking simulations were performed using AutoDock Vina [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref039" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acs.jcim.1c00203" pmid="34278794" pmcid="PMC10683950" count="1">39</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref040" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jcc.21334" pmid="19499576" pmcid="PMC3041641" count="1">40</citation>], griding the active site region (20 × 20 × 20Å), using the deprotonates Cys<sub>P</sub> (thiolate state). <sentence_start/>Were generated 15 positions per simulation. <sentence_start/>Each ligand orientation was analyzed using UCSF Chimera tool [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref041" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jcc.20084" pmid="15264254" count="1">41</citation>] to determine the best pose using as criterion the distance of the reactive Cys<sub>P</sub> and the α,β-unsaturated group of the compounds with maximum distance of 5.0 Å and also the position compared with ligands found in the crystallographic structures of Prx isoforms active site as H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (PDB code = 3A2V), benzoate (2V32 1HD2; 1OC3; 2V41; 1H4O) and tert-butylbenzene-diol (4K7O). <sentence_start/>The protein-ligand analysis interactions of the best poses were performed using the LigPlot+.
Results
Chemical characterization of compounds C1 and C2

Compounds <bold>C1</bold> and <bold>C2</bold>, isolated as white amorphous solids, displayed [M-H]<sup>-</sup> ion peaks in ESI-HRMS at <italic>m/z</italic> 259.1328 and 287.1322, respectively. <sentence_start/><sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra indicated the presence of 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic ring based on the signals at δ 6.84 (d, <italic>J</italic> = 8.9 Hz, H-6), 6.98 (dd, <italic>J</italic> = 8.9 and 3.0 Hz, H-5) and 7.21 (d, <italic>J</italic> = 3.0 Hz, H-3) for compound <bold>C1,</bold> and at δ 7.03 (d, <italic>J</italic> = 8.7 Hz, H-6), 8.15 (dd, <italic>J</italic> = 8.7 and 1.6 Hz, H-5) and 8.58 (d, <italic>J</italic> = 1.6 Hz, H-3) for compound <bold>C2</bold>. <sentence_start/>These different signals suggest the occurrence of hydroquinone and 4-hydroxylbenzoic unities in compounds <bold>C1</bold> and <bold>C2</bold>, respectively, as previously reported in metabolites isolated from leaves of <italic>P</italic>. <italic>crassinervium</italic> [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref042" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0031-9422(03)00299-1" pmid="12943774" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Despite these differences, <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra of both compounds showed similar signals attributed to 1-oxo-geranyl moiety at δ 1.62 (H-9’), 1.72 (s, H-8’), 2.18 (s, H-10’), 2.30 (m, H-4’), 2.20 (m, H-5’), 5.12 (t, <italic>J</italic> = 7.3 Hz), and 6.66 (s, H-2’). <sentence_start/><sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra of compounds <bold>C1</bold> and <bold>C2</bold> exhibited signals attributed to sp<sup>2</sup> carbons of geranyl moiety at δ 196.1/195.8 (C-1’), 115.0/118.8 (C-2’), 161.4/163.8 (C-3’) 124.2/122.7 (C-6’), and 132.9/133.0 (C-7’), as well as three methyl groups at δ 25.7 (C-8’), 17.8 (C-9’), and 20.1/20.4 (C-10’); Evaluation of inhibitory properties of compounds C1 and C2

To assess the inhibitory activity of compounds <bold>C1</bold> and C2, we employed the NADPH oxidation assay [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref029" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nchembio.935" pmid="22484541" count="1">29</citation>] using the recombinant AhpC from <italic>P</italic>. <italic>aeruginosa</italic> (PaAhpC) or <italic>S</italic>. <italic>epdidermidis</italic> (SeAhpC) and the heterologous Trx system from <italic>E</italic>. <italic>coli</italic>. <sentence_start/>Representative results of the PaAhpC, SeAhpC, EcTrx, and EcTrxR expression and purification procedures are shown in <bold>S7A-S7D Fig</bold>. <sentence_start/>As inhibition control, reduced samples of PaAhpC or SeAhpC were treated with NEM, a well-known and powerful cysteine alkylating agent that is able to annihilate peroxiredoxin activity [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref044" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.freeradbiomed.2009.08.022" pmid="19716412" count="1">44</citation>]. <sentence_start/>As expected for the samples subjected to NEM treatment, no peroxidase activity was detected to both enzymes as indicated by the initial rates of hydrogen peroxide decomposition when compared to the enzyme without treatment (<bold>Fig 3 and Table 2</bold>).

Mode of PaAhpC inhibition

To better understand the mode of inhibition, we used PaAhpC pretreated with compound <bold>C2</bold> (50 μM), the excess was removed and the enzyme was challenge with different concentrations of hydroperoxides (from 50 to 750 μM). <sentence_start/>Although the <bold>C2</bold> concentration of 50 μM is able to strongly inhibit the peroxidase activity of PaAhpC, if the mode of inhibition is a competitive behavior, the growing concentrations of peroxides may be able to shift the compound <bold>C2</bold> away from the active site and restore the peroxidase PaAhpC activity. <sentence_start/>Our results revealed that only a residual activity was observed (<bold>Fig 6A</bold>). <sentence_start/>Since the amount of inhibitor was not able to overwhelm the activity of all the enzyme population, the portion of the enzyme that had not reacted with the inhibitor would maintain its normal kinetics. <sentence_start/>The determination of kinetic parameters revealed that no significant effect was observed in the <italic>K</italic><italic><sub>m</sub></italic>. <sentence_start/>On the other hand, parameters as <italic>K</italic><italic><sub>cat</sub></italic> and V<sub>max</sub> were expressively impacted (<bold>Fig 6B; Table 4</bold>). <sentence_start/>This behavior is compatible with an irreversible inhibitor as expected by a thiol-Michael addition chemistry [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref029" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nchembio.935" pmid="22484541" count="1">29</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref049" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2174/092986711796391705" pmid="21651479" count="1">49</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref051" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/jm00084a012" pmid="1552501" count="1">51</citation>].

Investigation of Michael addition adducts formation

Some natural products identified as inhibitors of human Prx exert their biological activity via thiol-Michael addition reaction by alkylating the catalytic cysteines [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref029" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nchembio.935" pmid="22484541" count="1">29</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref030" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1089/ars.2016.6703" pmid="27650197" pmcid="PMC5510680" count="1">30</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref033" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.chembiol.2019.04.003" pmid="31130519" count="1">33</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Compounds <bold>C1</bold> and <bold>C2</bold> tested in this work possess functional groups able to perform a Michael addition, i.e., an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl group. <sentence_start/>However, while compound <bold>C1</bold> showed no significant inhibitory effect, compound <bold>C2</bold> was able to inhibit PaAhpC, suggesting that the form of inhibition may occur by other means.

To evaluate if the inhibitory mechanism of compound <bold>C2</bold> to PaAhpC occurs through the thiol-Michael addition, we performed non-reducing SDS-PAGE, taking advantage of the difference in gel migration of the protein in different oxidation states. <sentence_start/>When oxidized to disulfide, AhpC enzymes migrate as a dimer (~ 44 kDa) due to intermolecular disulfide bond formation. <sentence_start/>On the other hand, the reduced enzyme appears as a monomer (~ 22 kDa) [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref052" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jmb.2012.09.008" pmid="22985967" count="1">52</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Consequently, it is possible to evaluate not only the redox state of these enzymes but also if the inhibitor was able to react with cysteine residues involved in catalysis. <sentence_start/>If one of the two cysteines is covalently modified by an inhibitor, no intermolecular disulfide is expected to be formed if the enzyme is challenge with hydroperoxides, and the proteins are detected as monomers.

The functional importance of some residues identified in the docking procedures has been determined. <sentence_start/>It has already been shown that the Phe/Tyr residue at this position in peroxiredoxins is involved in the decamer stabilization of the enzyme, through an unconventional hydrogen bond with the catalytic triad Thr [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref022" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/antiox10071032" pmid="34202406" pmcid="PMC8300647" count="1">22</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref023" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/srep33133" pmid="27629822" pmcid="PMC5024103" count="1">23</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref059" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.isci.2021.103258" pmcid="PMC8571717" pmid="34765909" count="1">59</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref060" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acs.chemrestox.8b00346" pmid="30701970" pmcid="PMC7036284" count="1">60</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Additionally, Glu<sup>138</sup> would be related to conformational changes during the catalytic cycle [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref061" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/bi4011573" pmid="24175952" pmcid="PMC3932808" count="1">61</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Except for the Val<sup>45</sup> and Glu<sup>138</sup> of StAhpC that are substituted by Asn in PaAhpC, a residue with similar physicochemical properties, all the remaining interacting residues are strictly conserved among the two peroxiredoxins, which corroborates the feasibility of the docking analysis.

An important aspect about the mode of inhibition, which was irreversible, may have been related to the adoption of Michael with other groups such as the O and N atoms from the side chain of the catalytic triad Thr of Arg residues. <sentence_start/>The α,β-unsaturated carbonylic system is in close proximity to both reactive group residues of these amino acids, which are also more exposed than Cys<sub>P</sub> and involved in interactions to guide the substrates to catalytic cysteines (<bold>Fig 1</bold>). <sentence_start/>Nonetheless, these assumptions lack experimental support and the determination of PaAhpC structures with compound <bold>C2</bold> is needed to reach any meaningful conclusions.
Discussion

We tested two biosynthetic related natural products isolated from <italic>P</italic>. <italic>crassinervium</italic> as inhibitor of the AhpC from bacteria: 4-hydroxy-2-(3’,7’-dimethyl-1’-oxo-2’<italic>E</italic>,6’-octadienyl) benzoic acid (<bold>C1</bold>), and 4-hydroxy-2-(3’,7’-dimethyl-1’-oxo-2’<italic>E</italic>,6’-octadienyl) benzoic acid (<bold>C2</bold>). <sentence_start/>Both compounds possess three common structural aspects: 1) benzene rings, 2) an α,β unsaturated carbonylic system, and 3) a flexible tail (oxo-geranyl unity) that resembles long-chain fatty acids. <sentence_start/>The sole difference is a hydroxyl group at C-4 position in compound <bold>C1</bold> which is substituted by a carboxylic acid in compound <bold>C2</bold> (<bold>Fig 2</bold>). <sentence_start/>Therefore, it is reasonable to assume that the carboxyl group is involved in the inhibitory properties of compound <bold>C2</bold>. <sentence_start/>In fact, benzoic acids and derivatives have been found in some crystallized in different peroxiredoxin structures, suggesting that the carboxylic acid in the aromatic ring is a factor that may favor the stabilization of molecules in the active site [<citation rid="pone.0281322.ref056" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1006/jmbi.2001.4853" pmid="11518528" count="1">56</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref057" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1110/ps.073399308" pmid="18359859" pmcid="PMC2271159" count="1">57</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0281322.ref062" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0102300" pmid="25025339" pmcid="PMC4099364" count="1">62</citation>].
